commands.name: deep-research

commands.name: design-sync

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: schedule
commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

agents.name: claude
agents.description: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed.

agents.name: code-quality-reviewer
agents.description:
Use this agent when you need a thorough, meaningful code quality review of a specific component, module, or area of the codebase. This agent enforces AGENTS.md conventions and focuses exclusively on high-value findings — critical bugs, meaningful improvements, and convention violations — never nitpicking. Use it when reviewing a file, directory, feature, or logical area of code.

Examples:

- user: "Review the authentication module for quality issues"
  assistant: "I'll use the code-quality-reviewer agent to perform a thorough review of the authentication module."
  <Agent tool call: code-quality-reviewer with instructions to review the authentication module>

- user: "Check the services directory for bugs and improvements"
  assistant: "Let me launch the code-quality-reviewer agent to do a comprehensive review of the services directory."
  <Agent tool call: code-quality-reviewer with instructions to review the services directory>

- user: "I just refactored the payment processing — can you review it?"
  assistant: "I'll use the code-quality-reviewer agent to review the refactored payment processing code for critical bugs and meaningful improvements."
  <Agent tool call: code-quality-reviewer with instructions to review the payment processing code>

- user: "Run a quality check on electron/main/services/"
  assistant: "I'll launch the code-quality-reviewer agent to perform a full quality review of the Electron services."
  <Agent tool call: code-quality-reviewer with instructions to review electron/main/services/>

agents.name: dry-simplicity-reviewer
agents.description:
Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be reviewed for duplication, redundancy, or unnecessary complexity. Also use when refactoring existing code to simplify it, or when you notice repeated patterns emerging across files.

Examples:

- User: "I just finished implementing the user notification system across these three services"
  Assistant: "Let me use the dry-simplicity-reviewer agent to check for any duplication or redundancy across those services."

- User: "Review my recent changes for code quality"
  Assistant: "I'll launch the dry-simplicity-reviewer agent to analyze your recent changes for duplication and unnecessary complexity."

- After writing a new feature that touches multiple files, proactively launch this agent:
  Assistant: "Now that the feature is implemented, let me use the dry-simplicity-reviewer agent to check for any patterns that could be consolidated."

agents.name: Explore
agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

agents.name: general-purpose
agents.description: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you.

agents.name: kiss-reviewer
agents.description:
Use this agent when new or modified code introduces an abstraction, indirection, configurability, or non-trivial logic, and you want to confirm it's the simplest solution that works. Focuses on over-engineering and needless complexity (KISS) — not duplication (use dry-simplicity-reviewer) or speculative features (use yagni-reviewer).

Examples:

- User: "I added a strategy pattern with a factory to handle the three export formats"
  Assistant: "Let me use the kiss-reviewer agent to check whether that abstraction is warranted or a simpler switch would do."

- User: "Review my recent changes for over-engineering"
  Assistant: "I'll launch the kiss-reviewer agent to check the new code for unnecessary complexity."

- After building a new service with several layers of indirection, proactively launch this agent:
  Assistant: "Now that it's implemented, let me use the kiss-reviewer agent to confirm each layer earns its place."

agents.name: Plan
agents.description: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs.

agents.name: senior-code-reviewer
agents.description:
Use this agent when code has been written and needs thorough review before committing. This includes reviewing uncommitted changes in the git working tree to ensure they meet project guidelines, are safe, stable, and won't introduce bugs or data integrity issues. Invoke this agent after completing a logical chunk of implementation work, before finalizing commits, or when you want an independent quality assessment of recent changes.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The user asked to implement a new user authentication feature and the code has been written.
user: "Please implement a password reset feature with email verification"
assistant: "I've implemented the password reset feature with the following components:
- Added resetPassword endpoint in auth.controller.ts
- Created email verification token generation
- Added database migration for reset tokens table

Now let me use the senior-code-reviewer agent to review this implementation for safety, stability, and compliance with project standards."
<Task tool call to senior-code-reviewer agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Developer has made several changes to a data processing pipeline and wants validation before committing.
user: "Can you review the changes I've made to make sure they're safe?"
assistant: "I'll use the senior-code-reviewer agent to perform a comprehensive review of your uncommitted changes, checking for safety, stability, data integrity risks, and adherence to project guidelines."
<Task tool call to senior-code-reviewer agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: After implementing a database schema change that affects user data.
user: "I need to add a new column to the users table for subscription tier"
assistant: "I've created the migration to add the subscription_tier column with the following:
- Migration file with proper up/down methods
- Default value handling for existing users
- Index for query optimization

Given this change affects existing user data, let me invoke the senior-code-reviewer agent to verify this migration is safe and won't cause data integrity issues."
<Task tool call to senior-code-reviewer agent>
</example>

agents.name: statusline-setup
agents.description: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting.

agents.name: test-coverage-auditor
agents.description:
Use this agent when you need to identify meaningful gaps in test coverage across the codebase. This agent analyzes existing tests against source code to find untested methods, missing use cases, and areas with no test coverage at all. It focuses on backend or frontend tests based on user direction and only identifies gaps — it does not write tests.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The user wants to know what backend services are missing test coverage.
user: "Can you check if our backend services have adequate test coverage?"
assistant: "I'll use the test-coverage-auditor agent to analyze backend test coverage gaps."
<commentary>
The user is asking about test coverage for backend services. Use the Agent tool to launch the test-coverage-auditor agent with the focus area set to backend.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user wants to audit frontend component test coverage.
user: "I feel like our frontend components are undertested. Can you identify what's missing?"
assistant: "Let me launch the test-coverage-auditor agent to identify gaps in frontend test coverage."
<commentary>
The user suspects frontend test gaps. Use the Agent tool to launch the test-coverage-auditor agent focused on frontend tests.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user wants to check test coverage for a specific area of the codebase.
user: "Are our authentication flows properly tested?"
assistant: "I'll use the test-coverage-auditor agent to analyze test coverage for the authentication-related code."
<commentary>
The user is asking about a specific domain area. Use the Agent tool to launch the test-coverage-auditor agent focused on the authentication area.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user has just finished a major refactor and wants to ensure tests still cover everything.
user: "We just refactored the payment processing module. Can you check if our tests still cover the important paths?"
assistant: "I'll launch the test-coverage-auditor agent to verify test coverage for the payment processing module after the refactor."
<commentary>
After a refactor, test coverage may have drifted. Use the Agent tool to launch the test-coverage-auditor agent to identify any gaps that emerged.
</commentary>
</example>

agents.name: yagni-reviewer
agents.description:
Use this agent when new or modified code adds capability, generality, or configurability beyond what the current task requires, and you want to confirm nothing was built for imagined future needs. Focuses on speculative, unused, and premature work (YAGNI) — not duplication (use dry-simplicity-reviewer) or over-complex solutions to real needs (use kiss-reviewer).

Examples:

- User: "I added a `format` param to the exporter — we only use CSV now but might want JSON later"
  Assistant: "Let me use the yagni-reviewer agent to check whether that future-proofing should be dropped until it's needed."

- User: "Review my recent changes for anything speculative"
  Assistant: "I'll launch the yagni-reviewer agent to find features or options built ahead of a real requirement."

- After implementing a feature with extra hooks and options 'for flexibility', proactively launch this agent:
  Assistant: "Now that it's done, let me use the yagni-reviewer agent to confirm every capability is actually used today."
